sections.html:
Down in southern Dakota County, Farmington marks the metro's outer rim. Population is 25,425, up 7.4 percent since April 2020, spread over roughly 14.6 square miles. Lakeville borders it on the west, and Empire Township lies to the east.

The median owner-occupied home is worth $366,200, and 86.5 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, so a seller mostly competes with other single-family houses. The city has 8,313 households of 2.85 people each. Median household income is $123,673, median gross rent is $1,241 and the average commute is 27.7 minutes. Owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,175 a month in housing costs, and owners without one pay $781, a handy benchmark when a buyer asks what the house costs to carry.

County Highway 50 splits the town in two for most residents. The older downtown is south of it, newer subdivisions are north of it, and more growth is spreading east into Empire Township. A trail along the Vermillion River links downtown, uptown and the Empire-side neighborhoods, which is worth a line in any listing.

Before closing, phone Farmington Utility Billing (651-280-6883) and book a final meter reading. Water is not turned off when you move out, so the account runs until you end it.

  • Bills arrive quarterly and cover water, sewer, storm water and street lights.
  • Trash and recycling come from Dick's Sanitation, which takes cancellations at 952-469-2239.
  • An unpaid final bill is certified to the property as a special assessment, so a buyer's title company may hold money back at closing if the account is open.

Landlords should know that rental utility accounts stay in the owner's name, which means you close the account, not the tenant. Rental accounts that fall behind carry a late fee of 10 percent. Ask Utility Billing for the exact balance on your closing date instead of guessing from the last bill.

sections.h2: Schools and neighborhoods buyers ask about
sections.html:
Farmington is in Independent School District 192, which enrolls about 6,900 students. The attendance area also takes in eastern Lakeville and the surrounding townships, so confirm the district for your exact street before you write a listing.

Condition questions vary by area. Subdivisions north of County Highway 50 are mostly under twenty years old, while downtown houses are older and more likely to need updated systems. Main routes are Minnesota Highways 3 and 50 and Dakota County Roads 31 and 50.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Farmington house
sections.html:
• Agent listing: strongest when the house shows well and you can ride out inspections and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Do it yourself: skips the commission, though marketing, forms and haggling fall to you.
  • Cash buyer: fits inherited houses, deferred repairs, tenant-occupied rentals and owners behind on payments. The buyer accepts the house in its present state and the closing date can follow your schedule.

Whichever you pick, Minnesota Statutes 513.55 requires a written disclosure of known material facts before a purchase agreement is signed. Repairs are not part of that duty. Cash buyers take the house as it stands, while retail buyers often negotiate fixes after an inspection.

sections.h2: Filing the deed in Dakota County
sections.html:
Every Farmington deed goes through the county records office in Hastings. Walk-in filing needs an appointment at the Administration Center, and mailed packets go to 1590 Highway 55 in Hastings with a return envelope. Most parcels countywide are abstract property, so your title company will search the record before closing.

Minnesota's deed tax is the net sale price times 0.0033. A deed also needs a well disclosure certificate, or a line stating that the seller knows of no wells (Minnesota Statutes 103I.235). Before a deed is accepted, the county auditor checks for delinquent taxes (Minnesota Statutes 272.12). Recording charges are set by state law and posted on the county's fee page, so your title company can quote the total.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Dakota County bills in two installments (Minnesota Statutes 279.01). A missed half draws a 2 percent penalty on a homestead and 4 percent on other property, with monthly additions through December.

Dakota County property tax installments
InstallmentDue datePenalty if missed
First halfMay 152 percent homestead, 4 percent other
Second halfOctober 152 percent homestead, 4 percent other

The settlement statement usually divides the year's bill between buyer and seller by closing date. Search your parcel on the county website for open balances before you list. Homestead applications are due December 31.

If you owe back taxes, ask Dakota County Property Taxation and Records for the payoff amount. Keep your latest tax statement handy so you can confirm the parcel number and the amounts already paid.

The disclosure law does not make you fix the house first. It makes you say what you know. List any leaks, past basement water, aging systems and work in progress, and hand the list over before the purchase agreement. A cash buyer reads the same list and prices around it, so small fixes done only to sell are often wasted effort. A line item you disclose is far safer than one a buyer finds later.

sections.h2: Gathering what the title company needs
sections.html: Have your latest tax statement, the parcel number, any lease, and the keys and openers ready. If the house is a rental, add the utility account details. Because most parcels in the county are abstract property, expect the title company to order a search, so respond quickly if it asks about old liens or easements. Setting these items out early is what keeps a closing date from slipping.

sections.h2: How quickly can a sale close?
sections.html: With cash, you choose the closing date, and it often lands within a few weeks since no lender appraisal is needed. An agent listing usually takes more time. For either path, schedule the water meter reading in advance and ask the county for your tax payoff figure. On the day, the title company pays off any mortgage and taxes owed, and the deed goes to the records office in Hastings.

faqs.q: How quickly can I close on a Farmington house?
faqs.a: A cash purchase can close on a date you choose, frequently within a few weeks, since no lender appraisal is involved. Listing with an agent generally runs longer. For either path, book the water meter reading with Farmington Utility Billing in advance.

faqs.q: Do I have to make repairs before I sell in Farmington?
faqs.a: No. The disclosure statute asks for a written statement of material facts you know, and repairs are not part of it. Cash buyers take the house as it stands, and retail buyers often negotiate fixes after an inspection.

faqs.q: What happens to an unpaid Farmington utility bill after a sale?
faqs.a: It stays attached to the property. The city certifies unpaid water, sewer, storm drainage and street light charges as a special assessment, so buyers' title companies usually want the last bill settled. A final meter read keeps the number accurate.

faqs.q: Who files the deed for a Farmington sale?
faqs.a: Dakota County's records office in Hastings, normally through your title company. The deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price, and the deed needs either a well certificate or a no-wells statement. The state sets the fees.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Farmington rental while tenants live there?
faqs.a: Yes. Go over the lease terms with the buyer and your title company. Rental utility accounts stay in the owner's name, so plan to close yours on the sale date.
